newsitem.title: FRANCE: Campaign launched, Chirac yet to fire starter gun.
newsitem.headline: Campaign launched, Chirac yet to fire starter gun.

text.p: A snap election campaign effectively began in France even before President Jacques Chirac fired the starter's gun, with rival parties sparring ahead of his announcement expected on Monday.

Political sources said Chirac would put paid to a week of feverish speculation and announce in a televised address expected at eight p.m. (1800 GMT) that a two-round general election would be held on May 25-June 1 or June 1-8.

Chirac's office refused to confirm this. Opinion polls predict a close battle and the National Assembly, where the ruling centre-right has a massive majority, does not officially have to face the electorate until March 1998.

But political pundits said Chirac wanted to get the election out of the way now, rather than have to campaign next year at a time of possibly unpopular austerity measures to qualify France for a single European currency.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin accused him of political opportunism. "This dissolution is an admission of defeat, he told TF1 television.

"If the government had any confidence in the success of its policy, it would calmly wait for elections in a year," Jospin said, adding that Chirac was also worried about corruption probes rocking the ruling centre-right parties.

Justice Minister Jacques Toubon immediately responded by issuing a statement saying that Jospin was "manifestly embarrassed" by the prospect of an election and dismissing Socialist policies as archaic.

Amid apparently orchestrated leaks by pro-government politicians, Chirac's office was tight-lipped except to deny a report in the daily Le Monde that he was planning a sharp shift towards free market economic policies.

Le Monde said Prime Minister Alain Juppe would set out campaign policies on Tuesday including austerity moves, such as speeding up tax cuts and limiting the role of the state, to enable France to qualify for European monetary union.
Industry Minister Franck Borotra prepared the ground for an election announcement. "The government is cleaning up state finances. Can we lose eight months of reforms?" he said.
"We have to maintain and increase the pace of reforms and we have to adapt the calendar to European and single currency deadlines."
The European Union is due to decide early in 1998 which countries meet the criteria to join the single currency at its planned launch in 1999.

In a further cooling towards the single currency, Jospin said that if elected he would not introduce further austerity measures to stop the public deficit overshooting the three percent target needed to join the Euro.
But he added that he was still in favour of the Euro, an issue which has so far prevented an electoral pact with the Communists.
The centre-right has an overwhelming 478 members in the 577-seat National Assembly following its landslide defeat of a Socialist government in 1993.
Greens leader Dominique Voynet dismissed a snap poll as "manipulation" dreamt up by a government short on ideas. "Chirac is an eternal president-candidate," she said.
The presidency would not be directly affected by the vote. Chirac, elected in 1995, has five more years to serve but a left-wing victory could make him a premature lame duck.
An IFOP opinion poll published by the weekly Journal du Dimanche said a majority of voters were dissatisfied with both Chirac and Juppe and 59 percent would welcome an early general election.
It said 56 percent disapproved of Chirac's performance, against 55 percent a month ago, while 61 percent had a negative opinion of Juppe, against 60 percent a month ago.
